feed.title: Combined summary - 676-Byte Knowledge-Asymmetry UTXO Rescue and Stateless Lattice PQ-MPC for Legacy Supply Migration

entry.title: Combined summary - 676-Byte Knowledge-Asymmetry UTXO Rescue and Stateless Lattice PQ-MPC for Legacy Supply Migration
entry.summary: The migration of Bitcoin’s infrastructure to post-quantum cryptography introduces formidable challenges, particularly in the domains of institutional custodial key management and the protection of legacy UTXOs against quantum-enabled threats. Institutional custodians frequently rely on distributed signing servers, which must often restore keys from cold backups situated in segregated environments. This operational reality complicates the adoption of stateful hash-based post-quantum signature schemes because such schemes require meticulous counter synchronization. Failure to maintain strict counter alignment can result in catastrophic key compromise, thereby undermining the integrity and safety of custodial systems. A substantial segment of the Bitcoin supply—estimated at 34%—remains locked in legacy outputs. These outputs are susceptible to quantum attacks capable of recovering public keys or may be rendered inaccessible due to the scheduled deprecation of address formats. Previous proposals aimed at safeguarding these vulnerable funds, including Lifeboat and Dropkick, necessitated the publication of significant amounts of on-chain witness data, imposing heavy technical and economic costs on the blockchain. The Adaptive Quantum Migration Protocol (AQMP v2.0) represents a considerable advancement in addressing these issues. It leverages a knowledge-asymmetry approach for the emergency migration of UTXOs, thereby eliminating the need to publish raw elliptic-curve public keys. Instead, a post-quantum lattice key is derived using a combination of the BIP-32 parent chain code and the original derivation path. This architectural choice reduces the total on-chain witness size to just 676 bytes—a marked improvement over Lifeboat’s 3,420 bytes and Dropkick’s 3,904 bytes. The protocol accomplishes this compactness through an efficient composition of cryptographic elements: a 32-byte chain-code commitment, a 64-byte lattice proof transcript, a 164-byte Merkle inclusion proof, and a 320-byte non-interactive zero-knowledge proof of the destination lattice, all safeguarded by a 96-byte Dual-Commit XOR cycle that mitigates front-running risks during a bounded confirmation window. For custodial applications, AQMP v2.0 introduces a stateless threshold signing engine built upon Shamir secret sharing and Lagrange interpolation within a finite field. The use of synthetic HMAC-SHA3-256 nonces, deterministically bound to the message digest, share commitments, quorum configuration, and backup epochs, ensures that partial signatures remain secure against nonce reuse—even after system resets and key restoration events. Performance evaluations indicate consistent verification times across quorum sizes, ranging between 3.90 and 4.68 milliseconds. The integration of P2MR roots and optimized aggregation techniques enables a dramatic reduction in block witness data for threshold multi-party computation (MPC), shrinking requirements from nearly 4 MB per block to just over 11 KB under standard transaction volumes. Comprehensive technical specifications, reproducibility resources, and reference implementations are accessible through the [published paper](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24341314) as well as the [BIP draft repository](https://github.com/laudzakusuma/aqmp-protocol). The proposal actively seeks community input regarding the underlying security assumptions of BIP-32 chain codes and the practical effectiveness of the Dual-Commit XOR defense in mempool scenarios.
